8	# Climb batch 13, rung W: an `override` at equal parameter types, `override` on generic types, the revival-covering box
9	
10	Branch `wip/rung-walk-override`, cut from a1a75716a. Commits: 4e0833a4f (the tests), 7ea90f57d (walk), 6bfd27720 (the specification). `seed-worktree.sh` seeded the worktree: exit 0, "seeded from /home/user/fortress-base13 (a1a75716a) in 3 s".
11	
12	## 1. What changed, and why
13	
14	**The strict relation (Q2 of batch 12's rung W, at its strict default).**
15	
16	The chapter's rule:
17	- An `override` "overrides any inherited declaration ... whose parameter type, not counting the type of the self parameter, is a strict subtype of the overriding declaration's parameter type" (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:585-589`).
18	- "It is a static error if a declaration with the modifier override does not override any inherited declaration" (`:594-595`).
19	- A declaration at equal parameter types hides the inherited one by the inheritance rule's equal clause (`:521-527`). It overrides nothing.
20	
21	What walk did: `Constructor.checkOverrides` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/Constructor.java:569-608`) asked only `overriddenBy`: each inherited parameter type a subtype of the override's, equality included. So `object B extends A` with `override f(x: ZZ32)` over `A`'s `f(x: ZZ32)` loaded and printed `B`.
22	
23	What it does now: it also asks that not all parameter types be equal. The new `sameParameterTypes` (`:610-627`) reads two types as equal when each is a subtype of the other, as `FunctionalMethodMeets.inherited` does (`OverloadedFunction.java:1211-1233`).
24	
25	What is unchanged: `overriddenBy` (`Constructor.java:666`) and its other callers, `providedByTrait` (`:519`) and `FunctionalMethodMeets.inherited`. There the equal clause and the override clause act together, and what a type inherits does not change.
26	
27	**At an instance of a generic declaration**, equal parameter types still count as overridden (`owner instanceof GenericTypeInstance`, `Constructor.java:588`; `:595`).
28	- The landed check reads the `override` declarations of a generic trait's instance where an object without static parameters extends that instance (`providedByTrait` with its check on, `:269` and `:519-537`).
29	- An instance can make equal two parameter types that the declaration keeps apart. Example: `trait G[\T\] extends A[\T\]` with `override f(x: Any)` over `A[\T\]`'s `f(x: T)`. At the declaration it overrides, since `T` is a strict subtype of `Any`. `G[\Any\]` makes both types `Any`.
30	- The declaration is now checked at its static parameters (below), and there the relation is strict.
31	- At an instance the landed relation stays. It is the fallback for a declaration that walk can make no stand-in for.
32	- `tests/OverrideGenericInstanceEqualTypesWalk.fss` gates it.
33	
34	**The generic declarations (row 665's override half).**
35	
36	What walk checked: an `override` only in an object without static parameters (`Constructor.java:269`, under `if (declared)`) and in a trait without static parameters (`BuildEnvironments.java:874`).
37	
38	The new check:
39	- `BuildEnvironments.checkGenericOverrides` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/BuildEnvironments.java:886-899`) checks a trait, object or object expression with static parameters that declares an `override`. It checks it once, at its declaration.
40	- It checks through a stand-in: the type that stands for every instance, with a symbolic type for each static parameter (`symbolicInstance`, `:1048`). The Meet Rule check of the same declarations works the same way (`checkGenericFunctionalMethodMeets`, `:1034-1037`).
41	- `Constructor.checkTypeOverrides` (`Constructor.java:547-567`) checks the stand-in as a declared trait (`checkTraitOverrides`) or a declared object (`finishInitializing`, `:263-269`) is checked.
42	
43	Where it is called:
44	- in pass 3, for a generic trait (`BuildEnvironments.java:875`) and a generic object (`:592`);
45	- where a generic object expression (one in a generic function) is registered (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/env/ComponentWrapper.java:186`), beside the Meet Rule check.
46	
47	`declaresOverride` now takes the declarations (`BuildEnvironments.java:878-884`), so that the object and the object expression can use it.

An object expression's owner prints as `*objectexpr_ObjectExpr at .../OverrideNothingGenericObjectExpressionWalk.fss:10.20`.

51	**The revival-covering box.**
52	- Its last sentence (`Specification/basic/functions.tex:441-445`) and the sentence of the Appendix I entry's effect that repeats it (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:2627-2631`) said that the compiled checker covers inherited abstract methods "reading no comprises clause".
53	- They now say that it reads such clauses: concrete methods over the types that a trait lists together cover an abstract method over that trait.
54	- The entry records the correction in its Change (`changes.tex:2574-2582`), its reason in its Rationale (`:2607-2620`) and the replaced sentence in its Original text (`:2664-2672`). This is the form the entries already use for a revised box ("The box said at first ...; it now says ...", `changes.tex:1017-1032`).

122	## 3. Where the fix belongs, and the precedent
123	
124	Where it belongs:
125	- `explorations/coordinator/map/spec-to-implementation.md:221-223` puts walk's traits, methods and objects in `BuildEnvironments.forTraitDecl` and `forObjectDecl` and the environments that they build.
126	- Walk's load checks of `override` are `Constructor.checkOverrides` and its two callers (FACTS, "Walk refuses at load an object that leaves an inherited abstract method without a body").

147

The counter printed two lines: `PROBE-scan` before the test of the modifier and `PROBE-standin` after it. Direct walk runs:

## 3. Q2: an `override` with equal parameter types overrides

### 3.1 What landed

`Constructor.checkOverrides` (`Constructor.java:555-576`) refuses an own declaration with the modifier `override` of an object, or of a trait without static parameters, that `overriddenBy` (`:615-634`) relates to none of the declarations its immediate supertraits provide; a generic or unreadable inherited declaration of the name counts as overridden. `overriddenBy` asks that each parameter type of the inherited declaration be a subtype of the override's, equality included. So `object B extends A` with `override f(x: ZZ32)` over `A`'s `f(x: ZZ32)` loads. The same non-strict relation drops inherited declarations in `providedByTrait` (`:528-530`), and `FunctionalMethodMeets.inherited` folds the equal clause and the override clause into one test (`OverloadedFunction.java:1211-1233`). No ledger row gates the equal-typed case (no row's text holds it), and no test writes it; PLAN's Q2 entry is its only record.

### 3.2 The chapter's letter

"A method declaration may have the modifier override. Such a declaration overrides any inherited declaration with the same name and the self parameter (if any) at the same position, whose parameter type, not counting the type of the self parameter, is a strict subtype of the overriding declaration's parameter type. ... A declaration with the modifier override must override some inherited declaration. It is a static error if a declaration with the modifier override does not override any inherited declaration" (`traits.tex:585-595`; the frozen copy, `:529`, `:535`, the same). The inheritance rule's second clause (`:525-527`) is the complement: a declaration with equal parameter types hides the inherited one without overriding it. So an equal-typed `override` hides by `:525-527`, overrides nothing by `:589`, and is a static error by `:594-595`. The letter is unambiguous.

Its history makes it deliberate. The 1.0 release of March 2008 (`Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf`, its text extracted) holds `override` only in the grammar and in the calculus's judgement on method overriding, which is redefinition at equal types with no modifier; it has no paragraph on the modifier. The team's internal list asks, under "overriding (03/10/08)", after an example in which `B`'s `override m(x: Object)` widens `A`'s `m(x: ZZ)`: "Do we want to allow to have override when the parameter types of the two declarations are the same?" (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:156-184`). The paragraph was written after that question, with "strict", and the question was never marked answered. The chapter's note says the modifier itself was "not yet supported" (`traits.tex:15-16`).

### 3.3 The team's later word

None. The later restart holds no text on the modifier (the keyword list and the BNF only). Welterweight has no modifier and calls covering "a generalization of the notion of 'overriding'" (`Papers/Welterweight/static.tick:28`). The Dispatch paper: "in Fortress overriding is merely a special case of overloading because the type of the receiver object is taken into account" (`Papers/Dispatch/body.tex:789-792`). Nothing outweighs the chapter here.

### 3.4 The implementations

- The team's checker never read the modifier (no `isOverride` in `scala_src` at `a874948ac`); the team's walk read it by name, dropping an object's inherited declarations of that name (`Constructor.java:442-474` at `a874948ac`, `newOverrides`).
- The revival's checker reads inheritance by the chapter: `providedAndOverridden` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1651-1700`) tests equality first, `equivalentED`, and marks the pair `equal` without consulting the modifier; only then, `isOverride && subtypeED`, an override (`excludes`, `:1663-1671`). Its return-type check treats an `equal` pair as an overloaded pair, both ways (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala:662-691`). So the checker does not read an equal-typed `override` as overriding; it reads it as the equal clause. It has no check of the modifier at all, which is row 653's checker half, waiting on row 650. PLAN's Q2 entry, "Both paths read it as overriding", is exact for walk and not for the checker.
- Walk: as landed, non-strict in both the drop and the check.

### 3.5 The library and the tests

The library writes no `override`: none in `Library/*.fss`, `Library/*.fsi`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/` or `ProjectFortress/CompilerLibrary/` (the word occurs only in prose comments, `Library/Random.fss:22`, `:43`, `Library/ReflectiveQuickCheck.fss:107`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4164`). Redefinition at equal parameter types is everywhere in it without the modifier, `getter asString()` in every object for one. The team's tests write it to widen: `disp0.fss` (`Number` over `ZZ32`), `disp1.fss` (`Number` over `ZZ32`, `Any` over `T`). The revival's tests write it to widen (`OverrideInTraitWalk`, `FunctionalMethodMeetProvided`, `AbstractOverrideUndefinedWalk`, `FunctionalMethodOverrideOtherPathWalk`, `OverrideFunctionalMethodWiden`, `OverrideAbstractMethodWiden`, `XXXOverrideInheritedThroughOtherSupertype`, `XXXOverrideModifierCodeGeneration`, `XXXOverrideReturnTypeNotSubtype`, `XXXOverrideGenericReturnTypeNotSubtype`) or over an unrelated type to be refused (`OverrideNothingWalk`, `OverrideNothingInTraitWalk`, the generic expected failures). No program in the tree writes an equal-typed `override`; no program's verdict hangs on Q2, and none needs the lenience.

### 3.6 Verdict

The landed reading does not stand as a reading of the chapter. It is a lenience: a modifier the chapter refuses is accepted. It changes no program's run (the inherited declaration is hidden either way, by the equal clause), only which programs load. Nothing later than the chapter speaks, nothing in the library or the tests needs it, and the team wrote the sentence with the question in view. Row 614's decision 3, which the worker followed, says "the chapter's second clause already makes an equal parameter type not inherited, so the rung follows `FunctionalMethodMeets.inherited`, which is not strict" (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-walk-open-param/REPORT.md:193`). That is right about inheritance and silent about the check: that inheritance treats an equal-typed declaration and an overriding one alike does not make the first an override.

What should replace it: in `checkOverrides` alone, the strict relation, each parameter type of the inherited declaration a subtype of the override's and not all equal; `providedByTrait` and `FunctionalMethodMeets.inherited` unchanged, since there the equal clause and the override clause rightly act together. A test `ProjectFortress/tests/OverrideEqualTypesWalk.fss` keyed `load_exception_contains=does not override any inherited declaration` (an object with `override f(x: ZZ32)` over a trait's `f(x: ZZ32)`), written as the expected failure `XXXOverrideEqualTypesWalk` first, with a row for the lenience, until the next walk rung makes the check strict. Row 653's checker half, when row 650 lets it be built, keyed the same way; `providedAndOverridden`'s `equal` flag already separates the two cases (`STypesUtil.scala:1655-1657`). What it changes: nothing in the library, the tests or the demos.

The other way is to answer the team's question of 2008 with yes: `traits.tex:589`, "a strict subtype", becomes "a subtype", through the revision form (the Appendix I entry, the `\revision` callout, the front matter and a decision record), and both paths stay as they are. That touches the specification and both implementations' reading, so it is the curator's (POSITIONS, "Which decisions taken inside the work reach Pavol, and how."). The first way needs no decision: it is the standard as written.

### 3.7 Default

The record's default, (a) as landed, holds only if the text is revised. By the standard the default is (b), the chapter's strict reading; what is built today stays until the next walk rung, gated by a row and an expected failure.

A trait declaration contains a set of method declarations.
Syntactically, a method declaration begins with
an optional sequence of modifiers followed by
the method's name,
optional static parameters
(described in \chapref{trait-parameters}),
the value parameter with its (optionally) declared type,
an optional type of a return value,
an optional declaration of thrown checked exceptions
(discussed in \chapref{exceptions}),
an optional \KWD{where} clause
(discussed in \secref{where-clauses}),
a contract for the method (discussed in \secref{method-contracts}),
and finally an optional body expression preceded by the token \EXP{=}.
If a method declaration has the \KWD{getter} modifier,
it does not affect the behavior of a program; rather,
it documents that the method is intended to serve as a getter.
A \KWD{throws} clause does not include naked type variables.
Every element in a \KWD{throws} clause is a subtype of
\TYP{CheckedException}.


Method declarations can include the following special modifiers:
\paragraph{\KWD{getter}:}
A method declaration with the modifier \KWD{getter} explicitly declares a
getter method for a field, even in the absence of an actual field declaration.
\note{The following description is too confusing.  Reword it!!!}
If such a field exists, there is no implicit getter for the field.
An explicitly declared getter method must take no arguments and return a
result of the field's type.
A getter method must not throw any checked exception.
Getter names may not overlap ordinary method names.
A getter method must be invoked with the field access syntax:
%expr.id
\begin{Fortress}
\(\VAR{expr}.\VAR{id}\)
\end{Fortress}
where \VAR{id} is the name of the getter method.



\paragraph{\KWD{setter}:}
A method declaration with the modifier \KWD{setter} explicitly declares a
setter method for a field, even in the absence of an actual field.
\note{The following description is too confusing.  Reword it!!!}
If such a field exists, there is no implicit setter for the field.
An explicitly declared setter method must take a single argument---the
value being set---and return \EXP{()}.
A setter method must not throw any checked exception.
Setter names may not overlap ordinary method names.
A setter method must be invoked with the \emph{assignment syntax}:
%expr1.id := expr2
\begin{Fortress}
\({expr}_{1}.\VAR{id} \ASSIGN {expr}_{2}\)
\end{Fortress}


We say that a method declaration \emph{occurs} in a trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{declares} a method declaration that occurs
in that trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{inherits} method declarations from the
declarations of its immediate supertraits
except those method declarations
that are \emph{overridden} (as described later in this section) or
whose parameter type (not including the type of the self parameter)
is equal to the parameter type of a method declaration
that occurs in the trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{provides} the method declarations that it
declares or inherits.




There are two sorts of method declarations:
\emph{dotted method} declarations and
\emph{functional method} declarations.
Syntactically, a dotted method declaration is identical to a function
declaration.
When a method is invoked, a special self parameter is bound to the
object on which it is invoked.



A functional method declaration has a parameter named \KWD{self} at an
arbitrary position in its parameter list.  This parameter is not given a type
and implicitly has the type of the enclosing trait or object.

\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Method.c.tex}
\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Method.d.tex}
where \VAR{internalF} is a freshly generated name.
Functional method declarations may be overloaded with top-level function
declarations.
An abstract function declaration
(described in \secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations})
can be provided also for overloaded functional method declarations.
See \chapref{multiple-dispatch} for a discussion of overloaded
functionals in Fortress.

When a method declaration includes a body expression, it is called a
\emph{method definition}.
A method declaration that does not have its body expression is referred to
as an \emph{abstract method declaration}.
An abstract method declaration declares an \emph{abstract method};
any object inheriting an abstract method must define a body expression for the
method.  An abstract method declaration may include the modifier \KWD{abstract}.
It may elide parameter names but parameter

Method declarations that are overridden by some declaration are not
accessible.  They are not considered for overloading checks.

Partial overriding of an overloaded functional is allowed

A method declaration may have the modifier \KWD{override}.

The return type of the overriding declaration must be subtype of

A declaration with the modifier \KWD{override} must override
some inherited declaration.

entries.name: TaskCreate
entries.description:
Use this tool to create a structured task list for your current coding session. This helps you track progress, organize complex tasks, and demonstrate thoroughness to the user.
It also helps the user understand the progress of the task and overall progress of their requests.

## When to Use This Tool

Use this tool proactively in these scenarios:

- Complex multi-step tasks - When a task requires 3 or more distinct steps or actions
- Non-trivial and complex tasks - Tasks that require careful planning or multiple operations
- Plan mode - When using plan mode, create a task list to track the work
- User explicitly requests todo list - When the user directly asks you to use the todo list
- User provides multiple tasks - When users provide a list of things to be done (numbered or comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions - Immediately capture user requirements as tasks
- When you start working on a task - Mark it as in_progress BEFORE beginning work
- After completing a task - Mark it as completed and add any new follow-up tasks discovered during implementation

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Skip using this tool when:
- There is only a single, straightforward task
- The task is trivial and tracking it provides no organizational benefit
- The task can be completed in less than 3 trivial steps
- The task is purely conversational or informational

NOTE that you should not use this tool if there is only one trivial task to do. In this case you are better off just doing the task directly.

## Task Fields

- **subject**: A brief, actionable title in imperative form (e.g., "Fix authentication bug in login flow")
- **description**: What needs to be done
- **activeForm** (optional): Present continuous form shown in the spinner when the task is in_progress (e.g., "Fixing authentication bug"). If omitted, the spinner shows the subject instead.

All tasks are created with status `pending`.

## Tips

- Create tasks with clear, specific subjects that describe the outcome
- After creating tasks, use TaskUpdate to set up dependencies (blocks/blockedBy) if needed
- Check TaskList first to avoid creating duplicate tasks

subject.description: A brief title for the task

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

metadata.description: Arbitrary metadata to attach to the task

entries.name: TaskUpdate
entries.description:
Use this tool to update a task in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

**Mark tasks as resolved:**
- When you have completed the work described in a task
- When a task is no longer needed or has been superseded
- IMPORTANT: Always mark your assigned tasks as resolved when you finish them
- After resolving, call TaskList to find your next task

- ONLY mark a task as completed when you have FULLY accomplished it
- If you encounter errors, blockers, or cannot finish, keep the task as in_progress
- When blocked, create a new task describing what needs to be resolved
- Never mark a task as completed if:
  - Tests are failing
  - Implementation is partial
  - You encountered unresolved errors
  - You couldn't find necessary files or dependencies

**Delete tasks:**
- When a task is no longer relevant or was created in error
- Setting status to `deleted` permanently removes the task

**Update task details:**
- When requirements change or become clearer
- When establishing dependencies between tasks

## Fields You Can Update

- **status**: The task status (see Status Workflow below)
- **subject**: Change the task title (imperative form, e.g., "Run tests")
- **description**: Change the task description
- **activeForm**: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")
- **owner**: Change the task owner (agent name)
- **metadata**: Merge metadata keys into the task (set a key to null to delete it)
- **addBlocks**: Mark tasks that cannot start until this one completes
- **addBlockedBy**: Mark tasks that must complete before this one can start

## Status Workflow

Status progresses: `pending` → `in_progress` → `completed`

Use `deleted` to permanently remove a task.

## Staleness

Make sure to read a task's latest state using `TaskGet` before updating it.

## Examples

Mark task as in progress when starting work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "in_progress"}
```

Mark task as completed after finishing work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "completed"}
```

Delete a task:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "deleted"}
```

Claim a task by setting owner:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "owner": "my-name"}
```

Set up task dependencies:
```json
{"taskId": "2", "addBlockedBy": ["1"]}
```

taskId.description: The ID of the task to update

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

addBlocks.description: Task IDs that this task blocks

addBlockedBy.description: Task IDs that block this task

metadata.description: Metadata keys to merge into the task. Set a key to null to delete it.

+component OverrideEqualTypesWalk
+export Executable

+(* A method declaration with the modifier override whose parameter type equals the inherited declaration's overrides nothing, since an override's inherited parameter type is a strict subtype of its own, so the program is refused at load, under walk (traits.tex, section "Method Declarations"). *)

+end

+component PairsRunRangesWalk

+(* The library's Pairs loads, and runRanges joins its single ranges and range sets by BOXPLUS into the runs of true elements, merging two runs that one false element separates (Pairs.fss, runRanges and RunRanges). *)
+
+run(): () = do

trait RunRanges comprises { SingleRange, RangeSet }
  getter ranges(): List[\CompactFullRange[\ZZ32\]\]

object SingleRange(n: ZZ32) extends RunRanges
  getter ranges() = <|[\CompactFullRange[\ZZ32\]\] |>
  opr BOXPLUS(self, other: SingleRange) = SingleRange(n + other.n)
  opr BOXPLUS(self, other: RangeSet) = RangeSet(n + other.left, other.ranges, other.right)
end

object RangeSet(left: ZZ32, ranges: List[\CompactFullRange[\ZZ32\]\], right: ZZ32) extends RunRanges

      (q, qs) = other.ranges.extractLeft.get
      RangeSet(left, ps || <| p.lower:q.upper |> || qs, other.right)

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record

POSITIONS.md:94
- **The S1 form**, the layered form the team used for 1.0 and its 2009 draft: a labelled callout at each changed passage that prints in every build (not a `\note`); a revival section in Appendix I (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), each entry with the reason, the original sentences quoted with their path and line in the unrevised copy, and route C with what reversing to it would take; one paragraph in the front matter; the full reasoning in a repository document. The unrevised copy is called "the Working Draft of February 2011", in the team's own form, each citation giving the path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; Appendix I says once that the directory's name is misleading, since only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Appendix I's introduction says that the entries follow the revival's decisions, route A the first of them, each naming its own.

POSITIONS.md:93
- **Every change to the specification is recorded with its reason.** "our plan needs to update the spec with the change that we do and somehow properly record why we decided that way, so that there is no open discrepancy between the spec and our implementation that would be confusing to people. We need to preserve the original historic record somewhere in a document with our reasoning why we did the switch and preserve the option to go the route C." Every change takes the S1 form, an original-tree edit flagged as such; `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is never touched.

Specification/appendices/changes.tex:1298:\seclabel{revival-comprises}
Specification/appendices/changes.tex:2550:\seclabel{revival-covering}
Specification/basic/functions.tex:396:\revision{revival-covering}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said that the
Specification/basic/functions.tex:435:\revision{revival-covering}{The Working Draft of February 2011 asked here for a
\subsection{Traits with comprises clauses read at the level of values}
\seclabel{revival-covering}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{internal-types};
\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations}; a draft note in the subsection ``Export
Statements'' of \secref{components}; the effect of \secref{revival-comprises}.
\item[Change] \secref{internal-types} defines covering: a type covers another
when every value of the second is a value of the first; a type covers each of
its subtypes, and a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause is covered by the union
of its listed types; covering is not the subtype relation.
Its example concludes that $V$ covers $S \inter T$, where it concluded that
$V = S \inter T$, and a sentence says that a trait may stand between $S$ or $T$
and their listed types, so that $S \inter T$ is not in general equal to a named
type.
\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations} asks the argument types of the concrete
declarations to cover the argument type of the abstract declaration, where it
asked their union to equal it, and, in its example, for a definition for every
type listed in the \KWD{comprises} clause of \TYP{Molecule} or definitions that
together cover those types, where it asked for one for every immediate subtype.
Each of these four passages has a box.
The draft note says ``all its listed types'' where it said ``all its immediate
subtraits''; a draft note prints only in a draft build, so it has no box.
The effect of \secref{revival-comprises} no longer says that these passages are
not revised.
A correction of 9~October 2026 changes the last sentence of the box after the
example in \secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations} and the sentence of this
entry's effect that repeats it.
They said that the compiled type checker checks that an object's concrete
methods cover the abstract methods it inherits, ``reading no \KWD{comprises}
clause''; they now say that it reads such clauses to do so, so that concrete
methods over the types that a trait lists together cover an abstract method
over that trait.
The normative text is unchanged.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
on 29~September 2026 that the passages that read a \KWD{comprises} clause at the
level of types are restated at the level of values, which is how
\secref{trait-decls} reads the clause since its revision of 28~September 2026
(\secref{revival-comprises}).
The team's later Types chapter names covering beside subtyping and exclusion as
a relation between types, and says that an instantiation of a trait with a
\KWD{comprises} clause ``is covered by the union'' of the listed types
(\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines 36--38
and 384--390, in the revival's repository).
Welterweight Fortress, the type group's calculus of 2012, reads the clause at
the level of values and counts an abstract declaration as covered when it is
implemented for all the types comprised
(\nolinkurl{Papers/Welterweight/grammar.tick}, lines 21--22;
\nolinkurl{Papers/Welterweight/fig-covered.tick}).
Under that reading a trait with static parameters may stand unlisted between a
trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause and its listed types; an instantiation of it
is then a subtype of the closed trait and of no listed type, though every value
of it is a value of a listed type, so the passages' conclusions hold of values
and not of types.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md}
and \nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/comprises-type-level-judgement.md} in the
revival's repository.
The sentence that the correction of 9~October 2026 changes was false when it was
written: since 6~June 2012 the team's compiled type checker, testing whether an
abstract method's parameter type is a subtype of the union of the parameter
types of the concrete methods below it, tests whether the union of the types
that a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause lists is a subtype of that union
(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/AbstractMethodChecker.scala}
and \nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala},
in the revival's repository).
It accepts an object whose methods over the two types that a trait lists cover
an abstract method over that trait, and refuses the same object when the trait
has no \KWD{comprises} clause.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-walk-override/REPORT.md} in the
revival's repository.
\item[Effect] No example of this specification becomes invalid.
Covering is not subtyping: where an instantiation of a trait with static
parameters stands between $S$ and $T$ and their listed types, its value is a
value of $V$ but its static type is not a subtype of $V$, and the compiled type
checker refuses to assign it to a variable of type $V$; the interpreter, which
has no static types, runs such an assignment.
The compiled type checker checks, at each object declaration, that the
object's concrete methods cover the abstract methods it inherits, and reads
\KWD{comprises} clauses to do so: concrete methods over the types that a trait
lists together cover an abstract method over that trait; top-level abstract
function declarations run on neither implementation.
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/types-vals-vars.tex},
lines 568--570:
\begin{quote}
because of the \KWD{comprises} clauses of $S$ and $T$ and the \KWD{excludes}
clause of $U$, any subtype of both $S$ and $T$ must be a subtype of $V$.  Thus,
$V = S \inter T$.
\end{quote}
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/functions.tex}, lines 377--378:
\begin{quote}
Furthermore, the union of the argument types of the concrete declarations for
\VAR{f} must be equal to \VAR{T}.
\end{quote}
and lines 413--415:
\begin{quote}
For the latter, the programmer must provide a definition for every immediate
subtype of \TYP{Molecule}, or it is a static error.
\end{quote}
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/components/source-code.tex}, line
429, the words of the draft note's second item that changed:
\begin{quote}
provided that all its immediate subtraits are considered to have concrete
method declaration with that signature.
\end{quote}
The effect of \secref{revival-comprises}, the revival's text of 28~September
2026, ended:
\begin{quote}
The passages that read a \KWD{comprises} clause at the level of types, the
intersection of two traits with such clauses (\secref{internal-types},
\secref{more-specific-rule}) and the definitions an abstract function
declaration requires (\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations}), are not revised;
whether they are to be restated at the level of values is not settled.
\end{quote}
The box after the example in \secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations}, the
revival's text of 30~September 2026, ended:
\begin{quote}
The compiled type checker checks, at each object declaration, that the
object's concrete methods cover the abstract methods it inherits, reading no
\KWD{comprises} clause; top-level abstract function declarations run on neither
implementation of the revival.
\end{quote}
and the effect of this entry said the same in its words.
\item[Route C] The same under route~C: the reading of a \KWD{comprises} clause
at the level of values does not depend on the rule on instantiations.
\end{description}

\subsection{The Meet Rule for traits with comprises clauses}
\seclabel{revival-meet}

definition for every type listed in the \KWD{comprises} clause of
\TYP{Molecule}, or definitions that together cover those types, or
it is a static error.
\revision{revival-covering}{The Working Draft of February 2011 asked here for a
definition for every immediate subtype of \TYP{Molecule}.
Where a trait with static parameters stands unlisted between a trait with a
\KWD{comprises} clause and its listed types, the immediate subtypes and the
listed types differ; the type group's calculus Welterweight Fortress (2012) asks
for definitions for all the types comprised.
The compiled type checker checks, at each object declaration, that the
object's concrete methods cover the abstract methods it inherits, and reads
\KWD{comprises} clauses to do so: concrete methods over the types that a trait
lists together cover an abstract method over that trait; top-level abstract
function declarations run on neither implementation of the revival.}

72:- **The compiled type checker checks `nat` and `int` static parameters** (`compile-ladder/rung-nat-checker/REPORT.md`). A size is a symbol or a literal compared by equality, an unknown one an inference variable of its own (`_InferenceVarInt`, a third constraint track in `Formula`), with `keep-size-params` in `TypeSchemaAnalyzer`, kind-correct static arguments in `AbstractMethodChecker` and `FnNameInfo.boundsFor`, and sizes compared by `ExportChecker.equalIntExprs`. Arithmetic in a size and a `bool`, `dim` or `unit` parameter are refused by name; a size a call leaves unknown is refused at the call (POSITIONS, "Sizes"), stricter than a dead type parameter's `BOTTOM` (`scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1937-1940`), and in an overload set as "The compiled checker refuses a call whose most specific arm has a size the call cannot fix" below says. Gated by `compiler_tests/NatInferredChecker`, `NatWrittenChecker`, `NatMethodChecker`, `NatExportChecker` and `XXXNatMismatchChecker`.

content.content:
SpecData/tables/fortress-keywords examples tables ProjectFortress/demos/100.out:16: Just prior to jetting off to Austin last week, I started playing around with a mobile version of this site. While a personal blog is hardly a site that really needs one (unlike, say, an app with a proven mobile user-base like Twitter), I wanted to see what would be involved in re-factoring this design into something more fitting for a mobile environment. The first step was to create a mobile style sheet. For this I duplicated the CSS file I've already built for large screens, and started stripping out the style that doesn't work so well on a smaller screen. The layout was simplified into a more linear single column, and some elements were re-done to provide a larger target area for a maximum Fitts factor, and background images were dropped wherever possible to cut down on bandwidth demands. I tried building something that would work well on more mobile devices than just the iPhone, but given that it's my testing device, it works best on that platform for now. And while I was at it, I thought hey, why not do a TV style sheet too? I've got a Wii, it's got a great browser, and a low-res TV screen could benefit from the same kind of special attention given a mobile device. So I built one of those as well, doing things like increasing font size, increasing border widths, and stretching images to double their original size. But here's the thing about media-specific style sheets: the browser in question has to support them. Mobile Safari grabs all screen media style sheets, and ignores the handheld media type entirely. So despite good intentions, my efforts were wasted on it. And that's what led me down the road of user agent sniffing... Okay, let's get this out of the way up front: user agent sniffing sucks. Devices like the Wii and the iPhone have incredibly capable browsers that can render these sites the same as any desktop browser, so it's reasonable to assume users will want to do so from time to time. (And I suspect that's why Mobile Safari uses screen in the first place.) Forcing a specific version sucks... if done improperly. But when used well, and not mandatory for the user, I think it's not entirely evil. And it leads to other potential improvements beyond what CSS can provide, like selective content serving. The way to sensibly handle sniffing seemed to lie in providing an out: the mobile and TV versions of the site both have a special header on every page that provides a "regular site" toggle link. Any time someone wants to switch back to the regular site, the link is right there in front of them. And all versions now have toggle links in the footer to switch between different media types; given that I've seen this on multiple mobile sites, it feels like the site's footer is resolving into a standard place for where these type of switches ultimately belong. To make all this work, I had to bust out the PHP. I'll preface this by saying I'm hardly a proficient coder, so there are bound to be ways to optimize what I'm showing below. I started with a pair of arrays: a list of mobile browser user agent strings, and a second list of TV browsers. The latter is a bit light at the moment, due to my lack of knowledge of what sort of browsers are available for use on TVs. (And that underscores why having a media toggle is useful: if the browser in question isn't flagged by the sniff, the user can manually invoke the TV version.) // ========================== // media check // array of mobile devices $userAgentsMobile = array ( "Blackberry", "Blazer", "Handspring", "iPhone", "iPod", "Kyocera", "LG", "Motorola", "Nokia", "Palm", "PlayStation Portable", "Samsung", "Smartphone", "SonyEricsson", "Symbian", "WAP", "Windows CE", ); // array of tv devices $userAgentsTv = array ( "Nintendo Wii", "Playstation 3", "WebTV" ); Arrays in place, the next step was building a few functions to do things like comparing these arrays with the user's actual user agent string, and setting cookies to make these media types persist. More on the latter in a second. // this function takes two arguments: an array of user // agents, and a specific user agent. // it will then try to see if the specific user agent exists // within the array. If so, it will return true, otherwise // it returns false. function checkMediaType($uaList, $uaKnown) { // check user agent string against array // return true if found, or false if not found if(in_array($uaKnown, $uaList)) { return true; } else { return false; } } // this function takes one argument: a string value that // specifies a media profile. It will then set a cookie in // the user's browser. It returns the media profile value, // to be used as a variable later in the page function selectMedia($media) { setcookie ('media', $media, time()+31536000, '/'); return $media; } With those functions in place, the code below ended up being the core of my script. In the first major if statement, I'm checking to see whether a cookie is set; the cookie exists to avoid parsing the user agent arrays every single time the site is loaded. I doubt I'm saving that much time if any, given my currently very simple arrays. But I can see them growing over time, so it seems to make sense that this value should persist on the user's end once the user agent has been determined. But if no cookie is found, then I'm doing the actual sniffing. I check the user agent string against both the mobile and TV arrays, and then act on them if they match one or the other. If neither matches, I default to the screen version of the site. // show standard screen version by default $mediaVersion = "screen"; // toggle media version if cookie is set if (isset($_COOKIE["media"])) { if ($_COOKIE["media"] == "mobile") { $mediaVersion = selectMedia("mobile"); } elseif ($_COOKIE["media"] == "tv") { $mediaVersion = selectMedia("tv"); } elseif ($_COOKIE["media"] == "screen") { $mediaVersion = selectMedia("screen"); } } else { // if no cookie found, sniff media type then set cookie $knownUserAgent = false; // compare the device arrays against the // client's user agent $mediaTypeMobile = checkMediaType($userAgentsMobile, $_SERVER['HTTP_USER_AGENT']); $mediaTypeTV = checkMediaType($userAgentsTv, $_SERVER['HTTP_USER_AGENT']); // if media version is found, set a media type cookie // otherwise flag this browser as screen to save // time on future loads if ($mediaTypeMobile) { $mediaVersion = selectMedia("mobile"); } elseif ($mediaTypeTV) { $mediaVersion = selectMedia("tv"); } else { $mediaVersion = selectMedia("screen"); } } And then the last step is checking to see whether any of the media toggle links have been selected. If a user is viewing the mobile site and wants to switch over to the regular site, I need to re-set the cookie so their new preference persists. This is all done through simple query strings; the HTTP GET variable being checked for (media) can be invoked simply by adding ?media=mobile to the end of a URL or link. // override media version and set a new cookie // if they have selected a "show {media} site" link if ($_GET["media"]) { if ($_GET["media"] == "mobile") { $mediaVersion = selectMedia("mobile"); } elseif ($_GET["media"] == "tv") { $mediaVersion = selectMedia("tv"); } elseif ($_GET["media"] == "screen") { $mediaVersion = selectMedia("screen"); } } Now that the cookie exists and the $mediaVersion variable has a value, I'm all set. Anywhere in the rest of my site, I can use a simple if statement to filter out the specific media version I'm targetting, and selectively show or hide content for it. This is how I'm hiding my header photo from the mobile version, for example (simplified for clarity):
" width="505" height="243" alt="" />
I put together the entire set of functions and a couple of small demonstrations of selective content into a file you can grab. (live demo) And to finish, a couple of highlights from the alternate media versions of this site. The mobile version goes small by stripping out images where appropriate to save on download times; the header photo is gone, avatars on comment pages are gone, and most of the decorative PNGs have been removed or converted to CSS border properties. While the TV version goes big by doubling font size, increasing border widths, stretching the header image to fill the entire horizontal screen width, doubles avatar sizes, and using a higher-resolution version of the site's logo. Quick caveat: I've only had the opportunity to test the alternate media styles on a limited range of devices, and likely won't any time soon. Device testing is too hard if you don't already have access to a wide range of devices. I tried stripping out some of the more complex CSS tricks like overflow clearing and absolute positioning, so even my Treo doesn't make a horrible mess out of the site, but no guarantees. And the bonus question: why am I serving up the media versions with media profiles set to all? Simple reason: clicking through and viewing the TV-only version on a computer was seriously ugly, because it ignored the style sheet. As it should. But people will click through anyway, so that was problematic. Simple fix: media="all" Updated to include iPod Touch. Updated PHP for minor optimizations in response to comments. \section{Where Clauses}
\seclabel{where-clauses}

\note{The \KWD{where} clause syntax in this section is out of date.}

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{Where} &::=& \KWD{where} \{ \emph{WhereClauseList} \}\\
\emph{WhereClauseList} &::=& \emph{WhereClause}(\EXP{,}
\emph{WhereClause})$^*$ \\
\emph{WhereClause} &::=& \emph{Id} \emph{Extends}\\
&$|$& \emph{TypeAlias} \\
&$|$& \emph{NatConstraint} \\
&$|$& \emph{IntConstraint} \\
&$|$& \emph{BoolConstraint} \\
&$|$& \emph{UnitConstraint} \\
&$|$& \emph{TypeRef} \KWD{coerces} \emph{TypeRef}\\
&$|$& \emph{TypeRef} \KWD{widens} \emph{TypeRef}\\
\end{Grammar}


Static parameters may have constraints placed on them
in a \KWD{where} clause.
A \KWD{where} clause begins with
\KWD{where}, followed by a sequence of static
parameter constraints enclosed in braces \EXP{\{} and \EXP{\}},
and separated by commas.


A \KWD{where} clause may introduce new static variables, i.e., identifiers
for types and other static entities that may not be static parameters.
We use the term \emph{\KWD{where}-clause variables} to refer to
static variables that are not also static parameters.
The \KWD{where}-clause variables must be bound in a \KWD{where} clause.


A static parameter constraint is one of the following forms:
\begin{itemize}
\item a trait constraint consisting of the identifier of
a naked type variable, followed by \KWD{extends}
followed by a set of trait references which may include naked type variables,
\item a type alias (described in \secref{type-alias}),
\item an arithmetic constraint,
\item a boolean constraint,
\item a unit equality constraint,

Property declarations (described in \secref{property-decls}) can be freely
